title: Bimetallic MOF-based electrochemical sensors for detecting synthetic phenolic antioxidants: design strategies, workflow, and future directions
content: Synthetic phenolic antioxidants (SPAs), including tert-butylhydroquinone (TBHQ), butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA), butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT), and propyl gallate (PG), are extensively utilized to prevent lipid rancidity in processed foods. However, growing toxicological concerns regarding their potential hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and endocrine-disrupting hazards motivate the development of rapid and sensitive screening tools. Electrochemical sensors modified with bimetallic metal–organic frameworks (BMOFs) have emerged as attractive sensing platforms because of their atomic-level dual-metal coordination, tunable pore architectures, and abundant catalytic active sites. This review provides an evidence-based evaluation of BMOF-based electrochemical sensors for SPAs. We assess the literature against four criteria: (1) matched monometallic controls to separate bimetallic effects from conductive-additive contributions; (2) electrochemical evidence for the overall proton/electron stoichiometry and, where available, for the proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) pathway; (3) density functional theory (DFT) support for adsorption energetics and d-band modulation, where available; and (4) reported statistical comparison with chromatographic reference techniques (HPLC-DAD). By evaluating pristine BMOFs, conductive nanocomposites (rGO, CNTs, and MXenes), and BMOF-derived porous heterostructures against these criteria, this review identifies the gaps that must be closed to move laboratory proof-of-concept sensors toward regulatory-grade food-safety screening.
